Dirt
dert
n. (mud, filth of the streets; the image of a defeated enemy trodden down, and of what the restless sea casts up)
From Old Norse drit, excrement — a blunt word in origin, softened in modern English to mean soil. The Hebrew at Psalm 18:42 is tit, mud or clay; at Isaiah 57:20 the pair is rephesh va-tit, mire and dirt.

Biblical Definition

David uses the word for total defeat: “Then did I beat them small as the dust before the wind: I did cast them out as the dirt in the streets” (Psalm 18:42). The street of an ancient city was where refuse and mud collected, and to be cast out as the dirt of the streets is to be beyond any further consideration. Isaiah supplies the more searching image, and it is one of the most exact descriptions of the unregenerate condition in Scripture: “But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt” (Isaiah 57:20). Three things are said at once. The sea is troubled, in constant motion; it cannot rest, the incapacity being in itself and not its circumstances; and what its motion produces is mire and dirt brought up from the bottom. The verse immediately following is the verdict: “There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked” (Isaiah 57:21). This is not a threat of future trouble but a description of a present state. The restlessness is the punishment, and the filth cast up is what the restlessness produces — which is why the same chapter opens with God dwelling with him that is of a contrite and humble spirit.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines dirt as any foul or filthy substance, mud, mire, or dust — and figuratively as meanness or sordidness of character.

expand to see more

DIRT, n. Any foul or filthy substance; excrement; earth; mud; mire; dust; whatever, adhering to any thing, renders it foul or unclean.

2. Meanness; sordidness.

DIRT, v.t. To make foul or filthy; to soil; to bedaub; to pollute; to defile.

DIRTY, a. Foul; nasty; filthy; not clean; as dirty hands.

2. Mean; base; despicable; as a dirty fellow; a dirty employment.

Key Scripture

Psalm 18:42 — "Then did I beat them small as the dust before the wind: I did cast them out as the dirt in the streets."

Isaiah 57:20 — "But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt."

Isaiah 57:21 — "There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked."

Isaiah 57:15 — "For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones."

Modern Corruption

Restlessness is diagnosed as a condition to be managed rather than a symptom of sin, and Isaiah's verdict is treated as harsh instead of clarifying.

expand to see more

Isaiah 57:20 describes a state that a whole industry now addresses without ever naming its cause. The wicked cannot rest, and the modern account of that inability is chemical, circumstantial, or historical — anything but moral. Scripture does not deny that affliction, illness, and injury genuinely disturb a man; the Psalms are full of such disturbance in the righteous. It says something more specific: that there is a restlessness whose cause is the state of the soul before God, that it produces mire and dirt in a life, and that it is not curable by rearranging the circumstances, because the sea is troubled from within. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the therapeutic account in order to rebut it

The chapter itself supplies the remedy, and it is not a technique. Five verses earlier the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity says that He dwells with the contrite and humble spirit, to revive them. The order matters: God comes down to the low, and the wicked in verse 20 are the ones who have not been brought low. Augustine's sentence about the heart being restless until it rests in God is the classic summary of Isaiah 57, and the pastoral duty it implies is neither to dismiss a man's unrest nor to treat it only as a condition, but to ask the question the passage asks — whether the sea can rest at all while it is what it is.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tit, mud or clay — Psalm 18:42, Isaiah 57:20; rephesh, mire stirred up — Isaiah 57:20; chuts, the outside or street — Psalm 18:42.

expand to see more

Hebrew tit — mud, clay, dirt; Psalm 18:42 and Isaiah 57:20.

Hebrew rephesh — mire, what is stirred up from the bottom; Isaiah 57:20, its only occurrence.

Hebrew chuts — the outside, the street; the place where refuse gathered.

Hebrew garash — to drive out, to cast up; the verb of the sea casting up mire.

Old Norse drit — the blunt origin of the English word, softened over time.

Usage

"“I did cast them out as the dirt in the streets” — defeat beyond further consideration."

"“The troubled sea, when it cannot rest” — the incapacity is in the sea, not its weather."

"“There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked” — a description before it is a threat."
